[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Все три панели из оригинала, без перерисовки.* В примере Sardana et al. горизонтальный пунктир на панели **(a)** задаёт одну и ту же целевую потерю. На каждом токене запроса или ответа 7B экономит $2(13-7)\cdot10^9=12\cdot10^9$ FLOP. Значит, из округлённых чисел на рисунке получается порог примерно в 580 млрд токенов: $$ T_*=\frac{0.7\cdot10^{22}}{12\cdot10^9}\approx5.8\cdot10^{11}. $$ При двух триллионах токенов обслуживания 7B тратит на вывод $2.8\cdot10^{22}$ FLOP, а 13B — $5.2\cdot10^{22}$. The 50,257 rows of width 768 count once: 38,597,376 parameters. LLaMA-7B uses two independently learned rows for input `▁cat` and its output logit, as in the top panel. Its vocabulary is smaller (32,000), but with width 4,096 the two matrices contain 262,144,000 weights together. There is no learned position table: RoPE acts on Q and K inside each block. The [[#Shapes and parameters of the original models|full LLaMA count]] adds attention projections, FFN and normalizations. ### Where the answer comes from Take the pair from the GPT-1 chapter: “A cat sleeps” and “An animal rests.” GPT-1 sends both sentences and their separators through the decoder, then applies a trained head to the state at the final `Extract` token to produce three logits. Fine-tuning labels assign a meaning to each coordinate. The [original GPT-1 diagram](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf#page=4) shows this as `Task Classifier`, separate from the vocabulary output. A language model without that head can receive `Premise: A cat sleeps. Hypothesis: An animal rests. Relation:`. Generate a label or compare the probabilities of three continuations: ` entailment`, ` contradiction` and ` neutral`. Each starts with a space after the colon. If a label spans several tokens, its probability is the product of their conditional probabilities; the second token is scored after the first. This makes it possible to use the vocabulary projection without training a classifier. The GPT-2 paper studied text prefixes for tasks such as translation and reading comprehension. This sentence pair illustrates the format; it is not a reported GPT-2 result. In few-shot GPT-3, completed examples precede that pair, such as `Premise: The door is open. Hypothesis: The door is shut. Relation: contradiction`. Only the final pair has a blank label. Demonstrations use space in the window and change the token states in the forward pass. There is no optimizer step. The base LLaMA can be evaluated the same way. The evaluator still chooses the example order, the label strings and [[00 Учебник/06 Encoder, Decoder и Encoder-Decoder/06 GPT-3 — in-context learning#gpt3-candidate-scores|how to score candidates of different lengths]]. LLaMA accepts the prompt in [[00 Учебник/06 Encoder, Decoder и Encoder-Decoder/06 GPT-3 — in-context learning#gpt3-relation-shots|the same text format as GPT-3]], but encodes it with its own tokenizer. The three lines starting with `Premise:`, `Hypothesis:` and `Relation:` (no instruction or BOS) use 23 tokens, versus 20 for GPT-2. The continuation ` entailment` uses three tokens instead of two; ` neutral` and ` contradiction` still use one each. Scoring the whole first label now takes three conditional probabilities. The token count does not tell us which label the model will choose. ### How Natural Questions was evaluated In §3.8 of the GPT-2 paper, several question–answer pairs already preceded the test question. The prompt asked for a short continuation; the model did not receive a document containing the answer. The largest GPT-2 scored 4.1% exact match. The paper does not break out zero, one and multiple demonstrations, so 4.1% does not belong in a zero-shot column as defined in the GPT-3 paper. [Radford et al., §3.8](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf#page=7). GPT-3 and LLaMA varied the number of demonstrations. The figure from the LLaMA paper shows one. The prompt includes an instruction, a question answered by “Frank Sinatra,” and a new question ending in `A:`. The `Target` line below the rule is the answer for scoring and does not enter the prompt. With zero demonstrations, only the instruction precedes the test question. In the 64-shot condition, 64 completed pairs appear there. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpt-history-2026-11-09/llama1-figure3-natural-questions.png|Original Natural Questions prompt: the Frank Sinatra answer enters the prompt; Charles Darwin remains the reference answer.]] *Hugo Touvron et al., [LLaMA v1, Figure 3, Appendix A, p. 17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.13971v1#page=17). Original left panel (Natural Questions), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).* The LLaMA authors generated greedily, extracted a short answer, normalized case, punctuation, articles and whitespace, and compared it against the accepted strings. For example, if the continuation were `Charles Darwin, an English naturalist`, the text before the comma would match the reference after normalization. This demonstrates the scoring rule, not a generation run. | Base model | 0 demonstrations | 1 demonstration | 64 demonstrations | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | GPT-3 175B | 14.6% | 23.0% | 29.9% | | LLaMA 7B | 16.8% | 18.7% | 26.1% | | LLaMA 13B | 20.1% | 23.4% | 31.9% | LLaMA was evaluated on the 3,610-question Natural Questions test set ([Table 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.13971v1#page=4) and [Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.13971v1#A1)). The GPT-3 row is from [Brown et al., Table 3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2005.14165v4#S3.SS2). GPT-3 gains 15.3 percentage points from zero to 64 demonstrations with fixed weights. The published LLaMA 13B results are competitive with GPT-3 175B on this task, with about 13.5 times fewer parameters. These are results from two papers, not a matched-prompt run. They cannot isolate the effect of RoPE, training tokens or corpus composition. TriviaQA, on the right of the original Figure 3, differs in another way: LLaMA used a filtered development set; the 71.2% GPT-3 few-shot result was separately confirmed on the wiki-split test server. Those numbers should not be treated as evaluations on identical questions. ### What changes when examples are reordered? Zhao et al. evaluated GPT-3 2.7B on SST-2 sentiment classification. Four labeled reviews preceded the test review. The researchers permuted their order while holding the reviews, prompt template and weights fixed. They recomputed accuracy on the same evaluation examples for each permutation, and repeated this for ten sets of demonstrations. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpt-history-2026-11-09/zhao21c-figure2.png|GPT-3 2.7B accuracy on SST-2 across permutations of four examples in each of ten demonstration sets.]] *Tony Z. Zhao, Eric Wallace, Shi Feng, Dan Klein and Sameer Singh, [Calibrate Before Use, PMLR 139](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/zhao21c.html), [Figure 2, p. 3](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/zhao21c/zhao21c.pdf#page=3), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The original plot was extracted without changing axes or labels.* The horizontal axis is the set index, not the number of examples. Every set contains four. Dots within one column show the results for different permutations; the box marks the interquartile range. For the first set, the lowest and highest points lie near 54% and 93%. A reproducible four-shot comparison therefore needs the examples, their order and the prompt template. The plot measures GPT-3 on SST-2, not the variation to expect from LLaMA. ### When examples define a new label mapping A model that labels a review `positive` may already know what that word means. A correct prediction alone does not show that it learned a rule from the prompt. Pan et al. compare three labeling schemes to separate the hint in the class names from the input–output pairs. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpt-history-2026-11-09/pan-icl-figure1.png|Pan et al.'s Random, Abstract and Gold prompts. The last column gives the expected label for each.]] *Jane Pan, Tianyu Gao, Howard Chen and Danqi Chen, [What In-Context Learning “Learns” In-Context, Figure 1, p. 8298](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.527.pdf#page=1), Findings of ACL 2023. Original artwork, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).* In **Gold**, at the bottom, a favorable review gets `positive`. In **Random**, each demonstration label is drawn uniformly from `positive` and `negative`. The reference for the test review is unchanged. This measures what a model can infer from the text and class names when the demonstration labels do not provide a reliable mapping. **Abstract** keeps a consistent mapping within the prompt but replaces class names with digits. Suppose `0` marks positive reviews and `1` marks negative ones. The correct answer for a new favorable review is `0`. Swap the digits in every demonstration, and the correct answer becomes `1` while the review and model weights stay fixed. The authors choose a new label permutation per test example and omit terms such as `Sentiment` from the abstract templates. The middle row of the illustration retains the task name so the prompts can be compared visually. The labels are single tokens in these experiments, so the evaluator can compare their logits after the prompt. [Method: §§2–3 and Appendix B](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.527.pdf#page=2). ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gpt-history-2026-11-09/pan-icl-figure2.png|Six plots for GPT-3, LLaMA and OPT. Top: model size at 32 examples. Bottom: example count at fixed model size.]] *Pan et al., [Figure 2, p. 8300](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.527.pdf#page=3). All six original panels and their legend, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).* In the bottom row, the weights of each model are fixed. Moving from 8 to 32 demonstrations increases average **Abstract** accuracy from about 45% to 60% for GPT-3 175B, and from about 48% to 57% for LLaMA-65B. **Random** does not show that gain. The results average across 16 classification datasets; the error bars show variation across three templates. GPT-3 and LLaMA were evaluated on different numbers of examples, so compare the changes within a panel before comparing heights across families. The **Abstract** improvement shows that more pairs can help the model follow a supplied mapping. The plot does not tell us which layers recover it or which architectural component explains the difference between models. ### Training compute and inference compute In 2022, [Hoffmann et al., §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2203.15556v1#S4) compared Chinchilla (70 billion parameters, 1.4 trillion tokens) with Gopher (280 billion, 300 billion tokens) at comparable training compute. Chinchilla achieved lower held-out loss and did better on many tasks. LLaMA starts from that result but also considers the cost of using the trained model. Sardana et al. fix the target loss rather than the training budget in the comparison below. GPT-3 held training tokens fixed while varying model size. LLaMA asks what quality a smaller model can reach if trained longer, and what it then costs to run. On the [[#llama-pretraining-data|LLaMA training curves]], 7B loss keeps falling toward one trillion tokens. This shows that further steps still reduce training loss. It does not tell us how much inference would pay for those steps. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/llama-scaling-2026-11-09/sardana24a-figure1.png|Three panels compare 7B and 13B at equal loss: training cost, inference cost, and total cost for two trillion served tokens.]] *Nikhil Sardana, Jacob Portes, Sasha Doubov and Jonathan Frankle, [Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal, PMLR 235 (2024)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/sardana24a.html), [Figure 1, p. 2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlresearch/v235/main/assets/sardana24a/sardana24a.pdf#page=2). All three original panels, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).* The horizontal dashed line in panel **(a)** sets a common loss target. 13B reaches it at $4.5\cdot10^{22}$ FLOP and 7B at $5.2\cdot10^{22}$ FLOP. Before the first request, 7B has spent an extra $0.7\cdot10^{22}$ FLOP. Panel **(b)** shows how serving can make up the difference. Under the paper's approximation, a forward pass costs $2N$ FLOP per token for a model with $N$ parameters. On each input or output token, 7B saves $2(13-7)\cdot10^9=12\cdot10^9$ FLOP. The rounded numbers on the figure therefore give a break-even point near 580 billion tokens: $$ T_*=\frac{0.7\cdot10^{22}}{12\cdot10^9}\approx5.8\cdot10^{11}. $$ At two trillion served tokens, 7B spends $2.8\cdot10^{22}$ FLOP on inference and 13B spends $5.2\cdot10^{22}$. Adding training gives $8.0\cdot10^{22}$ and $9.7\cdot10^{22}$ FLOP, the totals in panel **(c)**. This is an equal-loss comparison, not a measurement of two released LLaMA models. Equal loss does not guarantee equal quality on a particular task. Comparing costs in money also requires input and output lengths, throughput on the chosen hardware and resource prices ([§2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.00448v3#S2), [§6](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.00448v3#S6)).
